doc.title: Red Holloway interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Younger players who sound like him, and trading licks
summary: He discusses Ricky Woodard and Johnny Griffin, and how musicians once shared licks freely.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Do you think there are young students out today that emulate you?

Ahhh, listen, you know what? I don’t know. There was a friend of mine — in Los Angeles there’s is a young fellow, he says, “He sounds like you.” I said, “Well no, he doesn’t have the sound.” He said, “No, but the stuff that he plays and the phrasing,” he said Ricky Woodard. I can’t see it, but I listen to Ricky and there is this saxophone player, what’s his name — Wilbur Brown. Now Wilbur Brown is a hell of a saxophone player. He lives in L.A. But he says, “Ricky Woodard sounds like you.” I say, “Well not for tone,” I say, “maybe he might have like some of the ideas.” Now I’ll tell you who sounds, we sound pretty close, Johnny Griffin and I. Because of the fact that one of the things about when I was young coming up, if I heard something on the radio and I copied it, I would call you up and say listen, meet me over so and so, and I’d show you this lick that I learned from maybe Don Byas or maybe whoever it was, Charlie Parker, and I would teach it to you. And when you learned something you’d call me up and tell me about it, and so we all did that, you know. I mean trumpet players, trombone players, it didn’t really matter, you know? But today you can ask a young musician something, well you know he’d go off on some other stuff, and you never get an answer. So I don’t know as though it’s a closely guarded secret or something.
